exports.1: We are sending Ssalongo, who has diagnosed generators by ear for thirty-one years and has never once needed to open the casing — give him a bicycle, a torch and four nights and he will walk you to the exact wall it is coming out of. If it turns out to be nobody's, he will teach forty of your residents to hum along with it in a key the council can live with, and by March it will be a choir and not a complaint.
exports.3: As I said before: answer it. We are sending the brass signal lamp off our old lake ferry and the two boys at the pier who still know the code, on the strict condition that the harbourmaster's first message is GOOD EVENING and nothing else — anything longer and you have begun a correspondence you will not be able to end.
exports.5: Chapati rolled hot around two eggs, cabbage and tomato, eaten standing in the street with one hand — we move four hundred thousand a night and we can spare three men, three griddles and the whole technique for nothing. It is not a meal and it is not between meals, which is precisely the hole your magazine fell into; the only rule is that the eggs are always two, never one.
exports.7: Nine days of guaranteed sun, forty of our drying racks on the next cargo flight, and eleven women out of the produce market who can turn ninety thousand of anything into something that keeps until Christmas. They will want half the dried weight and a chair each in the shade, and they will not want instructions.
exports.8: You cannot fight wind down its length, you cut it into rooms — we are sending four of the men who rig our market tarpaulins, who hang two acres of canvas every dawn in a place where the storms arrive sideways. They will stagger canvas walls across the avenue every forty metres so it stops being a barrel and starts being a chain of small still places, and they will hang the ropes on the outside, which is the part everybody gets wrong.
exports.9: Put a market on the far side and open it at four in the morning, so the bridge has traffic before anybody is awake enough to have an opinion about a showroom. We will seed it: thirty traders for one season, their airfare on us, on the condition that for the first year the bridge is the only permitted way in — a thing people are made to walk becomes a thing they say they chose.
exports.10: Send us the car park map and we will send you three of our boda stage chairmen, who allocate two hundred spaces a day out of a school exercise book with no lines painted on the ground and no appeals process. Your problem is not spaces, it is that nobody in your city can name the person who decided; give every street one chairman with a book and a face, and the arithmetic stops mattering within a month.
exports.12: Following on from the eggs — we have run market crèches since long before anyone wrote them down: a warm room off the trading floor, mats not cots, one woman awake per nine children asleep, opening at ten at night and closing when the mothers come off shift. We will send Mama Nakato, who has run ours for nineteen years, plus the rota book, the mat supplier and the pricing rule that made it work: it must cost less than a bottle of soda, or the grandmothers will simply keep doing it for free and resenting you.
exports.13: We volunteer. Our second-division side will travel to you every year at their own expense on the condition that they are permitted to be completely insufferable about it for the full ninety minutes, and we are sending the trophy with this letter: forty kilos, cast iron, genuinely ugly, and it lives with whoever lost.
exports.14: Sell the roof by the square metre and paint every buyer's name on the underside of it, in a good hand, big enough to read from the floor — we are sending Ronnie, who has lettered every shopfront on our main road for twenty years and can do eleven hundred names in a fortnight. People will not pay to fix a ceiling, but they will pay to be looked up at by their grandchildren, and a roof that everybody is named on gets its permits renewed by people who take it personally.
exports.15: Katogo: green banana and beans stewed together in one pot since midnight, ladled into a bowl you hand straight back, with black tea boiled hard with ginger. We can send you the cook, the pot and the three rules that make it work — open three till seven only, one price, and no seat facing the door, because people coming off the night do not want to be looked at.

answers.1: Camping. You own a bed. You own a roof. You paid for both of them, and then you drive out of town to sleep on the ground and tell me about it for a week.
answers.3: That I did the thing I said I would do. Everyone calls me energetic — my mother calls me energetic, and she does not mean it kindly.
answers.7: Plastic chair outside my cousin's hardware shop, seven o'clock, the man with the roast maize comes past and I always buy two and always eat both. Radio on inside, football or an argument about football, and people stopping to complain to me about a drain, which honestly I enjoy — you learn more in an hour on that chair than in a whole day of meetings. Home by ten, and the deal with my wife is that the phone goes in the fruit bowl.
answers.8: A boda stage chairman called Kizito, who has never held an office in his life and settles about forty disputes a day with no budget and no minutes. He taught me the entire job in one sentence: decide out loud, in front of everybody, and then do not move.
answers.10: Mombasa. I know the road, I know three people on it, and I would be selling something by Thursday.
answers.13: The back room in Nsambya, two beds for four of us, a green metal window that only ever opened halfway because of a nail nobody would take out. My aunt's sewing machine lived in the corner and was the most valuable object in the house; we were told not to lean on it, so naturally we all leaned on it. There was a calendar photograph of a fjord taped above the door and no one could tell me how it got there, and I decided at about twelve that I was one day going to stand in it. Still haven't.
answers.14: The top floor of the old post office. Nobody has been up there since the lifts died, so I take a flask and sit on the stairs for two hours. There's no signal, which was not the reason, but it is very much the reason now.
answers.15: The three quick taps a boda gives on the horn just before he passes you on the wrong side. Cheerful. Entirely unearned.
answers.16: A charger for a Nokia I lost in 2011. It is in the drawer. It will never be needed. It is not going anywhere.
